title: Yudhishthira stays put
hookLine: the brothers know the house will burn, and the son of Dharma weighs it: why Hindus call dharma subtle
carry: dharma is subtle, not a rulebook
tomorrow: who sleeps in the house the night it burns?
last: DHARMA PROTECTS THOSE WHO PROTECT IT.

cards: Bhima's answer is the obvious one. If this house is made to burn, let's get out of it, back to where we were safe. It's the answer that comes first, standing in a room that smells of fuel.
The walls look solid. The rooms are fine. Purochana is all smiles.
And somewhere in the plaster is enough to turn the whole place into a torch. Yudhishthira says no. We stay.

teach.h: IF WE RUN, HE BURNS IT NOW.
teach.b: Yudhishthira lays out his reasons. If we run, Purochana will know we've guessed, and he'll set the fire at once, or Duryodhana's people will hunt us down. We have no allies out here, no treasury, no army.
So we'll live here as if we suspect nothing. We'll go hunting, learn every road and path, and make a way out nobody can see.

teach.h: VIDURA'S DIGGER, AND A HIDDEN PASSAGE.
teach.b: Then help arrives: a skilled digger, sent by Vidura, who proves himself by repeating words from the riddle on the road. From the middle of the house he digs a passage out, and covers its mouth level with the floor.
Purochana keeps watch at the door, sure his guests know nothing. Now look at who made that call.

teach.h: THE SON OF DHARMA WEIGHS IT.
teach.b: Yudhishthira is the son of Dharma, the god of right order, and the most truthful of the brothers. You'd expect the rule-keeper to do the simple thing: accuse the liar, or walk out.
Instead he weighs it, and chooses to keep quiet, to keep his mother and brothers alive.

The Mahabharata has a phrase for moments like this, and it comes back again and again: dharma is subtle. Dharma is one of Hinduism's biggest words: the right way, the duty that holds a life and a world together.
And for Hindus it isn't a rulebook you look up. It's a weighing: who is at risk, what's true, what each choice sets off. Even the son of Dharma has to think.
So the brothers eat in the house, sleep in the house, smile at Purochana, and wait, the text says, a long time, with weapons close at hand.

how: Hindu teachers still quote the Mahabharata's line that dharma is subtle when a hard choice has no easy rule; Yudhishthira, called Dharmaraja, is the epic's picture of a man who has to weigh it.

o: a house built to burn, with a tunnel dug beneath it
a palace of red wax where the Pandavas were born
a festival hall built in Varanavata for Shiva

games.q: the son of Dharma decides — tap the pairs.
p: son of Dharma, chooses to stay

s: the Pandavas fled as soon as they smelled the lac
Yudhishthira argued that running would make Purochana burn the house at once.
the digger proved himself with Vidura's riddle
he repeated words only Yudhishthira had heard on the road.
in Hinduism, dharma is one fixed rulebook you look up
the Mahabharata keeps saying dharma is subtle: even Yudhishthira, the son of Dharma, has to weigh it.

games.q: a friend asks: if Yudhishthira cared so much about truth, wasn't it wrong to act like he suspected nothing? by the lac house, what fits?
o: dharma is subtle. he weighed it, and keeping his family alive came first that night.
yes. the son of Dharma should have accused Purochana to his face.
dharma stops mattering once someone is trying to kill you.
games.why: the epic doesn't treat dharma as one rule for every moment. Yudhishthira weighs who is at risk and what each choice sets off; many teachers read that weighing as dharma itself.

practice: Bring to mind one choice in front of you that isn't simple, where two good things pull different ways. If you pray, say Om softly three times first. If you don't, just breathe.
Then don't decide yet. Weigh it the way Yudhishthira did: who could be hurt, what's true, what each choice would set off. Let the body be calm while the mind stays awake.

wordCard.voice: The lac house. The brothers stay, calm on the surface, while Vidura's digger cuts a hidden passage under the floor.

orig.note: Sanskrit jatugṛha: the house of lac; this part of the poem's first book is named for it.

carryVoice: Your line: dharma is subtle, not a rulebook. Even the son of Dharma had to weigh it. Tomorrow, the night comes. See you then.
